overview: A rigorous, interview-focused masterclass in Data Structures and Algorithms designed for technical placement preparation and coding interviews at top tech companies. Covers Big-O analysis, fundamental and non-linear data structures, dynamic programming, graph theory, and algorithmic intuition.
prerequisites: Proficiency in one programming language (Java, C++, Python, or JavaScript)
Understanding of loops, functions, recursion basics, and memory allocation
Familiarity with discrete math concepts (sets, permutations, logarithms)

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between Array and LinkedList in terms of memory cache locality?
interviewQuestions.answer: Arrays allocate contiguous memory blocks, which allows the CPU hardware prefetcher to load adjacent elements into L1/L2 caches efficiently (high cache locality). LinkedLists allocate scattered nodes across heap memory with pointer chasing, resulting in frequent CPU cache misses and significantly slower sequential scans despite theoretical O(1) insertions.

interviewQuestions.question: Explain QuickSort worst-case time complexity and how to avoid it.
interviewQuestions.answer: QuickSort has an average complexity of O(n log n). However, if the pivot chosen is consistently the smallest or largest element (such as choosing the first element on already sorted data), partitions become heavily unbalanced (size 1 and n-1), resulting in O(n^2) worst-case time. It can be mitigated by choosing pivots randomly (Randomized QuickSort), using Median-of-Three pivot selection, or switching to Introsort.

interviewQuestions.question: How does Disjoint Set Union (Union-Find) achieve near O(1) time complexity?
interviewQuestions.answer: By combining two key optimizations: 1) Path Compression (flattening tree structure during find operations so every node points directly to the root), and 2) Union by Rank/Size (attaching the shallower tree under the deeper tree). This reduces time per operation to O(alpha(n)), where alpha is the Inverse Ackermann function, effectively constant (<= 4) for all practical universe scales.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you systematically approach a dynamic programming problem in an interview?
interviewQuestions.answer: 1) Define the subproblem in plain English (e.g. dp[i][j]); 2) Identify the base cases; 3) Formulate the state transition recurrence relation; 4) Determine the evaluation order (top-down memoization vs bottom-up table); 5) Analyze time/space complexity and optimize space (e.g. rolling array variables).
